content: The Know Your Epidemic approach, as part of second-generation HIV surveillance, emphasizes the importance of tracking HIV incidence to understand the trajectory of the epidemic and identify areas where new infections are emerging, both at national and subnational levels. Young pregnant women aged 15–24 years attending antenatal care (ANC) clinics are a key population for surveillance because they are likely to have recently initiated sexual activity, making their HIV infections more likely to be recent. Monitoring HIV prevalence trends among this group can provide valuable insights into HIV incidence trends when combined with other data sources. Sentinel surveillance, which uses data from specific sites, cannot be pooled to provide national or subnational estimates due to its non-probability design. However, if surveillance programs aim to achieve precise HIV prevalence estimates among young pregnant women at specific sites, sample sizes must be adjusted accordingly. This can be achieved through methods such as sample size inflation or oversampling, as detailed in the guidelines. Eligibility criteria for pregnant women included in surveillance should be clearly defined and adapted to the local context. Inclusion criteria typically include confirmed pregnancy, age 15–49 years, and attending their first ANC visit during the current pregnancy to avoid duplicate sampling. Exclusion criteria include women who have already attended an ANC visit during the current pregnancy or those outside the age range of 15–49 years. Eligible women are included regardless of their HIV status, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, or whether they received an HIV test at their first ANC visit. Retrospective data collection involves visiting ANC sites after the surveillance period to sample records of eligible women from routine data tools. Consecutive sampling is a simple and effective technique for selecting records, starting from the first day of the surveillance period and continuing until the required sample size is reached. Real-time data collection, on the other hand, involves ANC staff recording data during patient visits. This method allows for greater control over data quality and supports routine HIV and syphilis testing. However, it requires more resources and training for ANC staff and field coordinators. Real-time data collection is particularly useful in settings where the quality of routine program data is inconsistent. Surveillance data should be managed and stored securely, with encryption and password protection for electronic devices and databases. Personal identifying information should only be collected when necessary and permanently deleted once its purpose is fulfilled. Data entry and cleaning are critical to maintaining the accuracy and integrity of surveillance data. Best practices include using trained clerks for data entry, designing electronic data entry screens to match data collection tools, and performing double data entry to identify and resolve discrepancies. Regularly producing frequency tables for each site and variable can help identify and address data quality issues. Data analysis for HIV surveillance involves calculating site-specific prevalence by dividing the number of HIV-positive pregnant women by the total number of women with known HIV status. This includes both newly diagnosed and previously known HIV-positive cases. These methods can also be applied to calculate syphilis prevalence. In summary, effective HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC clinics requires clear eligibility criteria, robust data collection and management practices, and rigorous analysis methods. These efforts are essential for generating reliable estimates of HIV prevalence and incidence, which are critical for guiding public health interventions and monitoring the epidemic.
